prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My first week in Cambridge a car full of white boys tried to run me off the road, and spit through the window, open to ask directions. I was always asking directions and always driving: to an Armenian market in Watertown to buy figs and string cheese, apricots, dark spices and olives from barrels, tubes of paste with unreadable Arabic labels. I ate stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the mirror. The floors of my apartment would never come clean. Whenever I saw other colored people in bookshops, or museums, or cafeterias, I’d gasp, smile shyly, but they’d disappear before I spoke. What would I have said to them? Come with me? Take me home? Are you my mother? No. I sat alone in countless Chinese restaurants eating almond cookies, sipping tea with spoons and spoons of sugar. Popcorn and coffee was dinner. When I fainted from migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man above me mouthed: “No breakfast.” He gave me orange juice and chocolate bars. The color red sprang into relief singing Wagner’s Walküre. Entire tribes gyrated and drummed in my head. I learned the samba from a Brazilian man so tiny, so festooned with glitter I was certain that he slept inside a filigreed, Fabergé egg. No one at the door: no salesmen, Mormons, meter readers, exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, no one. Red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.

I ate stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the mirror afterward. The floors of my apartment never came clean, no matter how I scrubbed. Popcorn and coffee passed for dinner. When I fainted from a migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man leaning over me mouthed, “No breakfast,” then pressed orange juice and chocolate bars into my hands. The color red leapt into sharp relief as I sang Wagner’s *Walküre*—whole tribes seemed to gyrate and drum inside my head. I learned the samba from a Brazilian man so small, so festooned with glitter, that I was certain he slept curled inside a filigreed Fabergé egg. No one ever came to my door—no salesmen, no Mormons, no meter readers, no exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, no one. Only red notes, sounding through a gray trolley town.

---

During my initial week living in Cambridge, a carload of white teenagers attempted to force me off the roadway, hurling spit through their rolled-down window when I'd simply asked for directions. Direction-seeking became routine, as did my constant driving—often to Watertown's Armenian grocery, where I'd purchase figs alongside string cheese, apricots, exotic spices, and barrel-stored olives, plus paste containers marked with Arabic script I couldn't decipher. Grape leaves stuffed with filling became a regular meal, and afterward I'd examine my swollen lips in the mirror. No matter how much I scrubbed, my apartment's floors remained permanently dingy.

Spotting fellow people of color in libraries, galleries, or dining halls would make me catch my breath and offer a timid grin, yet they'd vanish before I could utter a word. What would there have even been to say? "Join me"? "Bring me somewhere familiar"? "Could you be my mother"? Instead, I dined solo across countless Chinese restaurants, nibbling almond cookies and drinking oversweetened tea. Some nights, dinner consisted merely of popcorn paired with coffee.

One episode of migraine-induced fainting occurred inside a supermarket, and a Portuguese man leaning over me silently mouthed the words "no breakfast" before handing me orange juice and candy bars. During performances of Wagner's Walküre, the shade of red would leap out vividly before my eyes, while entire imagined tribes seemed to dance and pound drums somewhere in my mind. A diminutive Brazilian man, dripping with sequins, taught me to dance samba—he seemed so ornately adorned that I imagined him nesting nightly inside some jeweled Fabergé shell.

My doorbell simply never rang: not for salespeople, not for Mormon missionaries, not for utility workers or pest control agents, not even for some modern Harriet Tubman. Just silence—red musical notes echoing through a colorless streetcar city.

# Finding My Way: A Season of Isolation and Discovery

The first week in Cambridge left an indelible mark on me, one that came not through the halls of academia but on an ordinary street. A group of white boys, perhaps emboldened by the anonymity of numbers or simply reveling in casual cruelty, tried to force me off the road as I walked. When that failed to satisfy whatever impulse drove them, they spat in my direction. I remember standing there afterward, shaken not just by the physical threat but by the stark realization of how visible and vulnerable I was in this new place—a place I had imagined might offer a fresh start, only to be reminded so quickly of old, familiar hostilities.

Despite this unsettling welcome, I continued to explore the city on my own, often driven by small missions that gave my wandering a sense of purpose. I sought out the specific tastes of home and heritage wherever I could find them, discovering an Armenian market tucked into the city's fabric where I could buy figs, olives, and fragrant spices. These excursions became a private ritual, a way of asserting my own cultural continuity even as I navigated streets that felt foreign and sometimes unwelcoming.

Yet solitude took on a different texture when I encountered other people of color in these public spaces. I found myself watching them with a kind of longing, hoping for some unspoken recognition, some gesture of solidarity between strangers who shared at least the experience of being marked as different. But I could never find the words. Whatever bridge I imagined building remained unbuilt, and I would walk away from these encounters feeling the isolation more acutely, as if proximity without connection only underscored how alone I truly was.

This period of emotional strain took a toll on my body as well. I was careless with myself in ways I didn't fully register at the time—skipping meals, losing track of the rhythms that keep a person grounded. The neglect caught up with me one day when I fainted from hunger, my body simply giving out from the accumulated deprivation. It was a stranger who noticed, who recognized the signs and brought me something to eat, restoring me with a small act of kindness that felt enormous in that moment of vulnerability. Their attentiveness was a quiet reminder that compassion could still find me, even in a city that had shown me its harsher face.

But amid this difficult season, there were also moments that broke through the isolation with startling intensity. Music had a way of reaching me when words could not—I remember being unexpectedly moved by Wagner, the swelling drama of the composition finding some corresponding chord within me, offering a kind of emotional release I hadn't known I needed. And then there was the samba, taught to me by an instructor whose flamboyance was infectious, whose joy in movement seemed to insist that my body, too, could be a site of pleasure and expression rather than only vulnerability. In these moments—through symphonic swell and rhythmic sway—I found glimpses of connection and vitality that reminded me I was still capable of being moved, of being alive to beauty even as I struggled to find my footing in an unfamiliar world.

# Cambridge

The first thing she noticed about Cambridge was the quality of the light—thin and gray, filtering through clouds that seemed to have taken up permanent residence over the city. It was nothing like home. Nothing about this place was like home.

Amara had arrived three weeks ago with two suitcases and a scholarship letter, expecting the university to feel like an arrival, a beginning. Instead, it felt like falling into water too cold to swim in properly, her limbs slow to respond, her breath caught somewhere between her chest and throat.

The flat she rented was small, tucked above a shuttered bakery on a side street whose name she still mispronounced. At night, she could hear pipes groaning through the walls, and sometimes she imagined they were speaking a language she used to know but had forgotten. She'd taken to leaving the radio on low, just for the sound of voices, even when the songs meant nothing to her—tinny British pop, cheerful and hollow, filling the silence she couldn't otherwise stand.

Food became her tether to something real. She'd wander into shops searching for the specific sharpness of scotch bonnet peppers, the particular sweetness of plantain, and when she found them—in a small Caribbean grocery run by a heavyset man named Winston who called everyone "love" indiscriminately—she'd buy more than she could carry, just to stand there a moment longer in the smell of it, the familiar spice cutting through the fog of displacement. Winston would sometimes slip an extra piece of ginger into her bag, wink, and say nothing. It was enough to make her chest ache with unexpected gratitude.

The university itself was a maze of ancient stone and unspoken rules. In seminars, she'd raise her hand and feel the room's attention shift toward her like a held breath, as though her voice itself was an interruption. A professor once corrected her pronunciation of a word she'd grown up saying, told her—kindly, he thought—that the *correct* way was different. She'd nodded, said nothing, and gone home to cry quietly into a bowl of rice she'd cooked herself, the only voice in the room her own.

There were moments of danger she didn't discuss with her mother on their weekly calls. The night a group of young men followed her from the bus stop, jeering words she pretended not to hear, her keys gripped white-knuckled between her fingers until she reached her door. The email from a classmate, thinly veiled in academic language, questioning whether she'd "earned" her place through merit or other means. She learned to walk faster, speak less, arrive early to empty rooms just to claim a small corner of space before anyone else could make her feel like an intruder in it.

But there were kindnesses too, small and unpredictable. An elderly woman on the train who shared her umbrella without a word, simply shifting closer when the rain began. A busker near King's College whose saxophone solos she'd stop to listen to on her way to the library, the notes bending in ways that reminded her of church back home, of Sunday mornings thick with harmony and sweat and her grandmother's hands raised high. She never learned his name, but she left coins in his case more often than she could afford, grateful for five minutes of feeling something other than alone.

She tried, for a while, to find groups—a Black student society that met sporadically, more performative than substantive, its members polite but distant, already absorbed into their own established circles. She attended twice, sat at the edges of conversations that didn't quite include her, and stopped going by the third meeting. There was no one asking her to stay.

Nights were the hardest. She'd lie awake listening to the city's peculiar quiet, the distant church bells marking hours she didn't feel forming into any recognizable rhythm. She missed the noise of home—horns, voices, music spilling from windows, the sense of life happening loudly all around her. Here, the silence felt like judgment, like the city itself was waiting to see if she'd last.

She didn't write home about the loneliness. Her mother had sacrificed too much for this opportunity, had wept with pride when the acceptance letter came. So Amara sent photos instead—of gothic spires, of punts gliding along the river, of herself smiling in a wool coat she'd bought to survive the cold. She didn't send photos of herself eating dinner alone at 9 p.m., the radio murmuring beside her, or of the ache that settled into her bones on Sundays when the whole city seemed to close its doors against her.

By the time spring came, threading pale green into the trees along the Backs, she'd learned to navigate the city with the ease of someone who'd stopped expecting it to open itself to her. She knew which streets to avoid after dark, which shops would serve her without hesitation, which professors' office hours felt safe to attend alone. She'd built a life of small competencies, careful survivals—but never quite a home. No one had shown her how to belong here, and she'd stopped waiting for someone to.

Still, she stayed. Still, she walked the cobblestones each morning past buildings older than her entire family's recorded history, the gray light settling over her shoulders like something she was slowly, painfully, learning to wear.

# Cambridge, Armenian Heritage, and Watertown: A Massachusetts Connection

The Greater Boston area, particularly the cities of Cambridge and Watertown, Massachusetts, holds a significant place in Armenian-American history and culture. This region became one of the most important centers of Armenian settlement in the United States, particularly following waves of immigration in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

**Historical Background**

Armenian immigrants began arriving in the Boston area in significant numbers in the 1890s, fleeing persecution in the Ottoman Empire. This migration intensified dramatically after the Armenian Genocide of 1915, as survivors sought refuge and new lives in America. Many settled in Watertown, drawn by employment opportunities in local industries, particularly at companies like the Hood Rubber Company, which employed many Armenian immigrants.

**Watertown: The Heart of Armenian Boston**

Watertown, in particular, became known as one of the most concentrated Armenian communities in the United States. The town developed a rich infrastructure of Armenian institutions, including churches, community centers, bakeries, and restaurants. St. James Armenian Apostolic Church, established in the community, became a cornerstone of religious and cultural life. Armenian bakeries, grocery stores, and restaurants along Mount Auburn Street created a distinctly Armenian commercial corridor that continues to thrive today.

**Cambridge's Role**

Neighboring Cambridge, home to Harvard University and MIT, also became intertwined with Armenian-American life. The city's proximity to Watertown meant that many Armenian families and institutions had connections spanning both communities. Cambridge's intellectual environment also attracted Armenian scholars and students, contributing to academic and cultural exchange.

**Cultural Legacy**

Today, the Armenian community in Watertown and Cambridge continues to preserve and celebrate its heritage through cultural organizations, the Armenian Library and Museum of America (located in Watertown), community festivals, and continued religious practice. This area remains a vital hub for Armenian diaspora culture, language preservation, and community support, representing one of the most successful examples of ethnic community establishment and preservation in American immigration history.

The Cambridge-Watertown Armenian community stands as a testament to resilience, cultural preservation, and the American immigrant experience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about being a Black or brown person feeling isolated and out of place while living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, full of vivid sensory details.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cambridge, Winter

The cold here has a different texture than the cold back home—it doesn't announce itself, doesn't warn you with thunderheads or the smell of rain coming. It just arrives, seeps through wool and skin, settles into the spaces between your ribs where you keep the parts of yourself you don't show at seminar. I walk past the brick facades of buildings older than my grandmother's grandmother's freedom, past windows glowing amber with the kind of warmth that seems to know it belongs there, and I count my footsteps like rosary beads, like evidence I still exist.

In the coffee shop on Mass Ave, the barista's smile doesn't quite reach past my shoulder, like she's looking for the person she expected to be standing here. The oat milk latte costs six dollars and tastes like belonging is something you can purchase if you just learn the right words, the right cadence, the practiced ease of ordering without an accent that makes heads turn. I say "thank you" too many times. I always say thank you too many times.

The Charles River holds its silence like a secret, gray-green and indifferent, sliding past joggers in their North Face jackets, their AirPods, their unbothered strides that have never had to consider which route home feels safest after dark. I press my palms against the railing, cold enough to burn, and I think about the rivers I've known that spoke different languages—rivers that smelled like fried plantain and diesel, that carried the sound of someone's auntie calling children in for dinner, that never once made me feel like a footnote in my own life.

In lecture halls with names carved in gold-leafed Latin, I learn to make myself smaller in ways that don't show on the surface—smaller in the pause before I speak, smaller in the way I explain my own experience like it's a foreign film requiring subtitles. The professor says "everyone" and means a specific everyone. The syllabus says "universal" and means a specific universe, one where my grandmother's hands, cracked from cassava and lye soap, don't appear anywhere in the citations.

At night, my apartment holds the only air where I exhale fully. I light candles that smell like nothing from this city—like red dirt after rain, like my mother's kitchen, like the ocean on the other side of the ocean I was born beside. I call home and my language comes back to me like a returning bird, easy and unpoliced, and for those minutes I am not translating myself, not editing my volume, not wondering if my laugh is too loud for these narrow streets built for other bodies, other histories.

The snow falls white and relentless outside my window, erasing color from everything it touches, and I think: how strange, how apt, that even the weather here practices its own kind of forgetting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness piece about loneliness and racial alienation in a New England college town, incorporating food, music, and strange encounters.
counterfactuals.output:
# Northampton, November

The dining hall smells like nothing I know—
some approximation of rice that isn't rice,
gravy the color of dishwater, and I think
of my grandmother's hands, the particular
music of oil hitting the wok, that hiss
like static between radio stations,
like the sound of not-quite-belonging.

Here, the leaves turn colors that have names
like *burgundy* and *auburn* and nobody
warns you about the cold that isn't just
weather but a kind of looking-through,
a professor's eyes sliding past you
to the window, the Berkshires blue-shadowed
and indifferent, and you are supposed to feel
lucky, aren't you? Scholarship kid,
diversity statistic, warm body
filling a number on a spreadsheet
somewhere in an admissions office.

*

Someone plays guitar in the quad—
folk music, all Dylan and dust,
and I don't have the vocabulary
for this kind of American,
though I've been here fourteen years,
though I dream in this language now,
though even my mother says
I sound different, sound *far*.

There's a boy in my seminar who asks
where I'm *really* from, and I want to say
*Ohio*, want to say *before that,
does it matter, does it ever stop
mattering*, but instead I smile
the smile I've practiced, the one
that costs nothing and gives everything back.

*

Late nights, I walk past the co-op
where the smell of patchouli and bread
makes something in my chest unknot
and then knot tighter, because this too
is a language I'm learning secondhand,
this New England quiet, these old stone walls
that held slaves once, held Puritans,
held generations of belonging
that I am borrowing, that I am
trying on like a coat two sizes wrong.

At the all-night diner, the waitress
calls me *hon* and doesn't ask
anything else, just pours the coffee,
and this small mercy undoes me
more than any solidarity statement,
any diversity panel, any well-meaning
question about my *experience*—

as if I could summarize it,
as if it fits between the sugar packets
and the napkin dispenser, as if loneliness
has a flavor I could name for you,
something between soy sauce and homesickness,
something like snow falling on a town
that doesn't know your name yet,
that maybe never will,

but here's the coffee, hon,
and here's the night going on and on,
and somewhere my grandmother is asleep,
dreaming in a language
I am slowly, slowly
forgetting how to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal narrative in the style of a prose poem about a young woman's first year living alone in Cambridge, mixing memories of racism, hunger, and unexpected kindness from strangers.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cambridge, First Year

The city gives you a key and calls it independence. You climb the stairs to a room the size of a held breath, and the radiator ticks like something counting down to nothing in particular.

Hunger arrives first, polite as an unwanted guest. It sits at your table shaped like an empty bowl, shaped like a bank account you check at 2 a.m., blue light on your face like a second, sadder moon. You learn the exact hour Sainsbury's marks down the bread. You learn which streets smell like other people's dinners, and you walk them anyway, coat pulled tight, pretending it's the cold making you shake.

Somewhere in October, a woman on Mill Road spits the word *Paki* at your back like it's punctuation, like it belongs at the end of an ordinary sentence, and you keep walking because your legs already know how to do this, have always known, since you were seven and the word first landed on you in a supermarket queue, your mother's hand tightening on yours like she could absorb it through skin. Cambridge with all its spires, its dead poets, its bicycles like a plague of black beetles — Cambridge does not exempt you. The stone is old. The old things it remembers are not always kind.

But then: the man at the market who presses free satsumas into your palm without being asked, says *you look cold, love*, as if cold were a language he could read on your face like weather. The librarian who doesn't mention the fine, who says *just bring it back when you can*, her kindness so plain it startles you, a coin found in an old coat pocket.

At night the room fills up with ghosts that are only your own thoughts wearing your grandmother's face. She is saying: *eat something.* She is saying: *they don't know who you come from.* The wallpaper peels in the corner like it's trying to show you what's underneath — plaster, brick, the bones of a house that has sheltered a hundred years of someone else's loneliness before yours.

You learn to cook lentils seven ways. You learn the Sunday bells don't mean anything except that another week has closed over you like water. You learn that a stranger's small mercy can sit in your chest for days, glowing faint as a nightlight, enough to walk by.

By spring the room no longer feels like a held breath. It feels like a held breath released — slow, uneven, but out. You have not stopped hearing the word. You have simply learned to set another word beside it: *satsuma. Library. Cold, love.* A ledger of small weights to balance the old ones.

The radiator still ticks. But you have started, some nights, to hum along with it, as if it were keeping time for a song you are only now learning the words to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an autobiographical-feeling prose poem that blends images of ethnic markets, classical music, and racial microaggressions to evoke displacement and longing for belonging.
counterfactuals.output:
# Market Music

I grew up between the smell of star anise and the sound of Bach's cello suites bleeding through my father's study door, two languages my body learned to translate before I understood either one belonged to me.

Saturday mornings meant the market on Argyle Street, where my grandmother's hands moved like conductors over bins of bitter melon, where the fish man called out prices in a dialect that lived only in that block, that hour, that particular slant of light through hanging ducks. I was fluent there in ways I couldn't be anywhere else—fluent in nodding, in knowing which vendor slipped extra scallions into the bag, in the choreography of elbows and baskets and *excuse me, excuse me* in three languages at once.

Then Monday: the school hallway, the orchestra room where I held my violin like a passport that kept getting questioned at the border. *You're so good at this for someone like you.* *Say something in Chinese.* *No, but where are you really from.* I learned to smile with my whole face while something folded quietly inward, origami of the self, smaller and smaller until it could fit in a pocket, unnoticed.

I have played Brahms in concert halls that smelled of nothing, sterile as a held breath, and felt more like myself than in rooms full of relatives speaking a mother tongue my mouth mangles like a foreigner. I have stood in the market holding mangosteens I didn't know the name for, aunties clicking their tongues—*you don't know this? what kind of Chinese are you*—while three blocks away, white classmates asked why my lunch smelled funny.

Where do you put a body that is asked to translate itself in every room it enters?

I think home might not be a place but a frequency—the particular hum of a cello's low string, the particular thwack of a cleaver through bone, the sound of my grandmother laughing at something I only half understood, and laughing anyway, because some things translate through the body before they reach the mind.

I am still learning to stop apologizing for the space I take up in either world. Still learning that longing itself might be the only inheritance that's fully mine—not the market, not the music, but the ache of standing between them, holding both, belonging to the ache instead of either shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic vignette in second-person-adjacent, first-person voice capturing a woman's solitary life in a mostly white city, weaving together sensory memories of food, dance, illness, and imagined community.
counterfactuals.output:
The city gives you its gray mornings like a gift you didn't ask for. You take the bus past faces that don't turn, don't nod, and you learn to make a home out of your own reflection in the window glass.

You cook the way your grandmother taught you, though she is a country away and thirty years gone. Rice that must hiss just so. Oil that must shimmer before the onions hit. You cook for one but you cook enough for six, because the body remembers hunger that isn't only about food—the ache for a table crowded with elbows, aunties arguing over the last piece of anything, a language that doesn't need explaining.

At night you dance in the kitchen with the shades drawn. You are seventeen again, sixteen, twelve—every age you've ever been, moving through you like water finding its level. The music is the only guest who never cancels. Your hips know things your mouth has forgotten how to say out loud in this town of polite distances, of *how are yous* that want no real answer.

The year your body betrayed you—fever climbing like something with intent, days blurring into a single gray smear—you lay alone and imagined hands that would have come, in another life, in another city that looked like you. Aunties with pots of soup. Someone to press a cool cloth to your forehead and click their tongue at your foolishness for not calling sooner. Instead: the hum of the refrigerator, the particular silence of a phone that might ring.

You built the community in the spaces between real things. The woman at the corner store who says your name right on the first try becomes, in your private mythology, someone who might notice if you disappeared. The recipe you post online, captioned for people who will never taste it, is a kind of prayer sent out into the ether—*does this look like home to you, too?*

Still, some mornings, the light comes through the window amber and forgiving, and you let yourself pretend the whole city is humming the same song you are, that somewhere close, someone is cooking the same meal, moving to the same rhythm, aching the same particular ache—and for a moment, before the illusion thins, you are not alone. You are simply early. Still waiting for the others to arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
